Variants.Content: A ship starts with wood selection. Solid long logs are suitable for the keel, bent timbers become the ribs, planks need to be dried, spliced ​​and caulked with flax and rosin; nails, anchor chains, ropes, canvas, masts and rudders come from different craftsmen and origins. Longships, merchant ships and warships have different requirements for speed, load and draft, and cannot be replaced at will by the same drawing. The lord can order the construction of ships, but he cannot shorten the growth of wood and the training of craftsmen by order; maintaining old ships is also very costly. A true fleet is the result of forests, mines, workshops, money and years of experience.

The shipwright first looks at the wood grain and seams, and the sailor then tests it with wind and waves. No matter how beautifully painted the ship is, if the keel is twisted or the caulking is jerry-rigged, it is just an expensive coffin.
Lords like to count new ships, admirals are more concerned with crews, repairs and supplies. A fleet without skilled sailors is just a row of wooden husks waiting to be dispersed by the wind.

The foresters saw good trees being cut down, the merchants saw orders, and the people along the coast saw work and conscription. The glory of shipbuilding often comes from those far from the coast who first contributed the wood and labor.
